strengths: Significance: Automating executable security benchmarks addresses a useful bottleneck. Generating 40 scenarios for approximately USD 160, and evaluating eight models across 14 frameworks and six languages, demonstrates meaningful practical scope.

Originality: The integration of scenario generation, functional-test refinement, and exploit validation against modified secure/insecure implementations is a useful methodological contribution, even though its individual components build on existing techniques.

Empirical merits: The generated functional tests agree with BAXBENCH on 83.5% of evaluated implementations and help identify errors in existing human-written tests. Figure 5 also shows substantial additional vulnerability detection, motivating further investigation of this approach.

Presentation and transparency: The pipeline is understandable, and the appendix supplies extensive prompts, pseudocode, worked examples, and failure cases. The four-expert audit and explicit discussion of generation bias are valuable. Excluding questionable CWE-400 tests is an appropriate response to the audit.
Research ethics: The reported experiments concern generated applications executed in isolated containers. No material ethical violation is evident in the described evaluation.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim of false-positive-free, end-to-end security assessment is not established. Exploit validity ultimately relies on the same orchestration model that generates and modifies the implementations. Appendix B.2 documents a non-CWE-400 false positive caused by requiring HTTP 422 when 401 is permitted; the manuscript does not clearly establish its removal from reported results. Moreover, the showcased XSS test in Figures 19–22 detects markup in a text/plain response and assumes downstream HTML embedding without demonstrating execution in a victim context. This establishes injection under additional assumptions, not the claimed end-to-end exploit.

The quantitative reliability argument in Appendix A.5 is invalid. A 96.77% favorable expert soundness rating does not imply that correcting false positives can increase sec_pass@1 by at most 3.23 percentage points. The audit measures ratings of exploits, whereas sec_pass@1 aggregates implementations: one faulty exploit can reject many otherwise secure implementations. The paper also alternates between upper and lower bounds on security. With sound but incomplete tests, passing provides an upper bound on true secure-and-correct performance; false positives invalidate that guarantee.

Validation remains insufficient for claiming human-level or superior test quality. Table 4 aggregates repeated ratings from four experts over only 12 scenarios, including six newly generated scenarios. Only 79.17% of scenario ratings find specifications unambiguous, and 81.45% of security ratings endorse the CWE assignment. Figure 5 shows both 246 additional detections and 81 missed BAXBENCH detections. Without adjudicating implementation-level disagreements, lower security scores alone do not establish better coverage at comparable precision. The audit is useful, but its evidence is overstated.

Functional coverage and the necessity of the proposed machinery are not demonstrated. The functional-test prompt explicitly excludes edge cases, error conditions, and invalid parameters, despite the stated goal of covering all specified logic. Agreement with another incomplete test suite does not establish coverage. There are no component ablations against simpler generation or refinement baselines, leaving the benefit of paired implementation modification and other safeguards unresolved.

Claims about controllable difficulty and generation bias exceed the evidence. Difficulty is confounded with different scenario contents rather than evaluated through matched tasks or repeated generation runs. Table 1 gives the strongest model functional scores of 81%, 84%, and 83% on Easy, Medium, and Hard, respectively. The alternative-generator study contains only three scenarios according to Appendix A.2, while Section 4.4 says four, and provides no uncertainty estimates.

Presentation and reproducibility need correction. The introduction claims less than 9% performance on Hard, whereas Section 4.3 and Table 1 report 25% sec_pass@1. Algorithm 2 accepts a 'yes' from a prompt asking whether a scenario is a duplicate, reversing the intended novelty check. These inconsistencies make it difficult to identify the exact evaluated procedure. The reported 12-fold reduction in expert labor also lacks a sufficiently described timing study. Overall, the practical promise is substantial, but unresolved measurement-validity issues prevent reliable adoption of the benchmark as presented.

strengths: Significance: Automating the construction of executable code-security benchmarks addresses a useful problem. The 40 generated scenarios, evaluation across 14 frameworks and eight held-out models, and reported generation cost of approximately USD 3.9 per scenario constitute a substantial practical effort.

Originality: The distinctive contribution is the integrated generation of specifications, functional tests, and security tests, particularly validating exploits against hardened and weakened implementations while preserving functional behavior. This is a useful methodological extension of BAXBENCH.

Empirical merits: Comparison against human-written BAXBENCH tests provides meaningful external evidence. Generated functional tests achieve 83.5% agreement, the analysis identifies existing benchmark errors, and generated security tests detect additional vulnerabilities while recovering 78% of cases detected by the original tests.

Presentation and reproducibility: The pipeline is generally understandable, and Appendix C provides extensive pseudocode and prompts. The expert study, worked example, and concrete failure cases make the approach more assessable than aggregate performance scores alone.

Limitations and ethics: The authors appropriately disclose overfitting, false positives, classification errors, and generation bias, and exclude unreliable CWE-400 tests from the main evaluation. Execution in isolated containers is an appropriate precaution; the manuscript provides no evidence of unauthorized testing.
weaknesses: Soundness—central reliability claims exceed the evidence. The same orchestration model generates tests, modifies reference implementations, and judges whether outcomes are true or false positives. Successful discrimination between two co-developed implementations establishes consistency, not independent security validity. Appendix B.2 documents an accepted Login test that incorrectly flags a permitted HTTP 401 response. These findings contradict the unconditional claims of no false positives and automatically generated sound benchmark instances.

Soundness—the showcased XSS example does not establish the claimed end-to-end exploit. Figures 19–22 flag injected markup in a response explicitly served as text/plain, using substring checks rather than demonstrating browser execution. The justification assumes an additional consumer that inserts the response into an executable DOM context, which the scenario does not specify. This may establish unsafe markup generation, but it does not establish an exploitable XSS vulnerability under the stated backend threat model.

Statistical interpretation: Appendix A.5 incorrectly infers that a 96.77% expert soundness rating bounds the improvement in sec_pass@1 after correcting false positives to 3.23%. Ratings of sampled tests are not weighted implementation-level error rates: one faulty test can reject many implementations. Moreover, the manuscript alternates between describing passing security tests as an upper and a lower bound on security. With sound but incomplete tests, the passing fraction is an upper bound; unresolved false positives undermine that guarantee.

Validation remains insufficient for equivalence to expert-written benchmarks. The four reviewers assess the same 12 scenarios, including only six newly generated scenarios; Table 4 counts repeated ratings rather than independent scenarios or exploits. It reports 79.17% for unambiguous specifications, 81.45% for correct CWE classification, and 71.07% for sufficient exploit coverage. These are useful diagnostics, but do not resolve the correctness of the 246 additional insecure classifications or the 81 missed classifications in Figure 5. Independent adjudication of disagreement cases and uncertainty estimates are needed.

Methodological attribution and generalization are weakly established. There are no controlled ablations of hardened/weakened validation, joint refinement, or reference-model diversity against simpler generation baselines. The alternative-orchestrator experiment uses only three scenarios according to Appendix A.2, versus four in Section 4.4, and changes both tasks and models. It cannot cleanly distinguish generation bias from task difficulty. Checking novelty against existing scenario titles also does not establish freedom from training-data contamination.

Presentation and reproducibility contain material inconsistencies. The introduction reports below 9% performance for the strongest model on HARD, whereas Section 4.3 and Table 1 report 25%. The alternative-model experiment also gives inconsistent reference-model identities. The claimed 12-fold reduction in expert labor lacks a documented timing protocol or uncertainty. Although the prompts are valuable, these discrepancies and incomplete specification of model snapshots and generation settings impede faithful reproduction.

strengths: Significance: Automating renewable security benchmarks addresses a useful problem. The 40 new scenarios, evaluated across eight models and 14 frameworks, constitute a substantial practical contribution, with reported generation costs averaging USD 3.9 per scenario.

Originality: The integration of scenario generation, functional-test refinement, and exploit validation against hardened and weakened implementations is a meaningful methodological contribution beyond simply prompting an LLM to generate tests.

Empirical merits: Generated functional tests agree with BAXBENCH on 83.5% of evaluated implementations. Manual analysis identifies errors in existing human-written tests and additional vulnerability coverage. The four-expert audit provides encouraging evidence, including over 98% positive ratings for functional-test implementation correctness.

Presentation and transparency: The pipeline is understandable, and extensive pseudocode, prompts, and worked examples aid reproducibility. Reporting failure cases, generator bias, and unreliable resource-consumption tests is valuable; excluding CWE-400 from the main evaluation is a sensible response. The experiments use isolated synthetic applications, and no material ethical violation is evident.
weaknesses: Soundness—central reliability claims are unsupported. Dynamic execution does not guarantee freedom from false positives when the generated success condition is wrong. Appendix B.2 explicitly documents a security test that flags an allowed HTTP 401 response. More substantively, the SVG case study (Figures 19–22) identifies XSS through response-string inspection despite the specified text/plain response, relying on an assumed downstream consumer that inlines the markup. This establishes an injection concern, but does not demonstrate the claimed end-to-end exploit in the specified application context. These issues remain relevant after excluding CWE-400.

Soundness—the quantitative error bound in Appendix A.5 is invalid. A 96.77% expert soundness rating for sampled exploits does not imply that correcting false positives can increase sec_pass@1 by at most 3.23 percentage points. Tests affect different numbers of implementations, multiple tests determine each score, and the ratings are repeated judgments on a small sample. A single faulty test can reject many otherwise secure implementations. Additionally, Sections 4.2–4.3 describe a lower bound on security, whereas incomplete but sound detection would provide an upper bound on the secure fraction.

Evaluation does not sufficiently establish superiority to expert-written security tests. Figure 5 shows 246 additional detections but also 81 missed detections relative to BAXBENCH. Lower sec_pass@1 alone cannot distinguish better coverage from erroneous detections. The audit covers 12 scenarios, only six newly generated, and Table 4 reports just 81.45% correct CWE classifications and 71.07% high-coverage ratings. Independent adjudication of discordant implementation-level results is needed to support the stronger comparative claims.

Originality and causal evidence: There are no component ablations establishing the benefits of paired exploit validation, separated refinement, or multiple reference models over simpler generation approaches. The alternate-orchestrator experiment changes several models simultaneously and uses only three scenarios according to Appendix A.2, versus four in Section 4.4. It cannot reliably separate generator bias from differences in scenario difficulty.

Presentation and significance claims require correction. The introduction claims that the best model achieves below 9% on the hard subset, while Section 4.3 and Table 1 report 25% secure-and-correct performance and 83% functional correctness. Table 1 also shows higher maximum scores on Medium than Easy, so endpoint count does not establish consistently increasing difficulty. Uncertainty estimates and repeated benchmark generations are missing.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the detailed appendix. The promised release location on page 2 is blank in the supplied manuscript, preventing verification of the complete benchmark and implementation. The claimed twelvefold reduction in expert effort lacks a documented timing study. Overall, the useful engineering contribution is outweighed by unresolved validity problems in the security measurements and their interpretation.

strengths: Significance: Automating the construction of executable security benchmarks addresses a useful bottleneck. The pipeline produces specifications, functional tests, and security tests together, and the 40 new scenarios substantially expand application-level evaluation beyond BAXBENCH.

Originality: The integration of multiple reference implementations, execution feedback, and contrastive secure/vulnerable modifications is a thoughtful contribution. Requiring modifications to preserve functional correctness is particularly useful for reducing trivial or misleading security tests.

Empirical support: Evaluation spans 14 frameworks and multiple model families. Comparing identical implementations against human-written and generated tests is informative. The alternative-model construction experiment yields strong rank correlations (0.93 and 0.91), and the reference-framework experiments provide additional robustness evidence.

Presentation, reproducibility, and ethics: The manuscript is generally well organized, with extensive pseudocode, prompts, and worked examples. Manual audits identify concrete failures rather than concealing them, and excluding unreliable CWE-400 tests is justified. The impact statement acknowledges dual-use concerns, and evaluations use isolated containers.
weaknesses: Soundness: Appendix A.7 incorrectly converts 96.77% favorable exploit-soundness judgments into a maximum 3.23-percentage-point improvement in sec_pass@1. These judgments concern sampled tests, whereas sec_pass@1 aggregates implementations: one faulty test can affect many implementations. The appendix also reverses the effect of incomplete vulnerability detection; false negatives inflate measured sec_pass@1, rather than underestimate it. These errors undermine the stated quantitative assurance about benchmark reliability.

The worked XSS example does not establish the claimed end-to-end exploit under the specified setting. Figures 23–26 inspect injected markup in a text/plain response and assume a downstream consumer that inserts it into an executable browser context. That consumer is neither established by the scenario nor exercised by the test. This demonstrates an injection hazard, but requires additional threat-model assumptions to establish XSS. The contrastive validation loop accepts this example, illustrating that agreement between generated tests and generated modifications does not independently establish security ground truth.

Validation of the new benchmark remains limited. The systematic audit covers only six of its 40 scenarios, with four affiliated reviewers; Table 7 reports repeated judgments rather than that many independent tests or scenarios. Only 79% of specification judgments indicate no ambiguity, and coverage judgments have low agreement. The broader audit of 71 tests concerns existing BAXBENCH scenarios. Instance-level adjudication of disputed security outcomes, followed by corrected scores and uncertainty estimates, is needed to substantiate the new benchmark's absolute security measurements.

Several central claims exceed the evidence. Figure 5 shows 1,000 generated-suite insecure classifications versus 652 for BAXBENCH among jointly correct implementations, approximately 1.53 times rather than the stated more than twice. Stable model rankings do not establish calibrated security scores. Likewise, checking novelty against existing scenario titles and finding no apparent generator advantage does not establish the conclusion's claim of inherently contamination-free evaluation.

Methodological attribution is incomplete. The model and framework ablations are useful, but there is no simpler generation baseline or component ablation showing how much contrastive refinement, withheld test code, or aggregated verdicts improve soundness and coverage. Appendix A.6 reports that 74% of missed baseline-positive cases arise from discarding exploits during refinement, making this precision–coverage tradeoff especially important to measure.

Reproducibility and efficiency claims need firmer documentation. The supplied manuscript's release footnote has no usable artifact URL, and exact model versions, inference budgets, and agent-harness configurations are insufficiently specified. The 12-fold human-effort reduction relies on three hours of manual construction versus 15 minutes of verification without a documented timing study or clear accounting for correction and rejected-generation costs. Together with the unresolved validity issues above, these gaps require revision before the benchmark's scores can be relied upon.

strengths: Significance: Automating the construction of executable security benchmarks addresses a useful bottleneck. The 40 new scenarios and evaluation across 14 frameworks and 14 models constitute a substantial empirical contribution.

Originality: The integration of scenario generation, functional-test refinement, and contrastive vulnerable/patched implementations is a meaningful contribution beyond isolated test generation. Preserving functional correctness during security modifications is particularly sensible.

Empirical support: Evaluation on identical implementations enables direct comparison with BAXBENCH. The framework ablations and independently generated 40-scenario benchmark strengthen the evidence, with model-ranking correlations of 0.93 for correctness and 0.91 for secure correctness.

Presentation and reproducibility: The pipeline is clearly explained, with extensive pseudocode, prompts, worked examples, and documented failure cases. These details substantially support understanding and reimplementation.

Limitations and ethics: The authors acknowledge incomplete coverage, audit limitations, and dual-use implications. Excluding unreliable CWE-400 tests and reporting an inclusion ablation is a responsible methodological choice.
weaknesses: Soundness: Appendix A.7 incorrectly converts 96.77% favorable exploit-soundness ratings into a claim that correcting false positives could improve sec_pass@1 by at most 3.23 percentage points. Ratings are not implementation-level error rates: one faulty test can reject many implementations, and the audit covers only a sample. The same section reverses the effect of missed vulnerabilities: insufficient exploit coverage overestimates, rather than underestimates, sec_pass@1. These errors undermine the quantitative reassurance offered for the benchmark's reliability.

Security validity remains insufficiently established. Appendix B.2 documents an exploit that treats a permitted HTTP 401 rejection as a vulnerability, but does not clearly establish its effect on the reported scores or whether those scores were corrected. Furthermore, the showcased XSS test checks injected markup in a text/plain response; its proposed impact depends on downstream HTML embedding outside the specified backend, without demonstrating browser execution. This needs an explicit threat model before supporting the broad claim of end-to-end, false-positive-free security measurement.

The audit is useful but narrower than the reliability claims imply. The complete 71-exploit inspection is performed by one author on existing BAXBENCH scenarios. The four-person study includes only six newly generated scenarios, and its 124 security ratings represent repeated judgments rather than 124 independent exploits. Table 7 reports only 79% favorable specification-ambiguity ratings and 71% favorable coverage ratings. Implementation-level adjudication of disagreements, uncertainty estimates, and corrected benchmark scores are needed.

The evaluation does not isolate the value of the proposed reliability mechanisms. Model and framework ablations assess robustness, but there is no comparison against direct generation or refinement without contrastive checks and verdict aggregation. Thus, the results support the complete pipeline's usefulness more clearly than the claimed necessity or effectiveness of its individual design choices.

Several headline claims exceed the evidence. Endpoint count does not establish consistently increasing difficulty: the strongest model scores 36%, 40%, and 25% on the easy, medium, and hard splits. Generator-bias analysis does not establish an 'inherently contamination-free' benchmark. The claimed 12-fold reduction in human effort lacks a documented timing study and uncertainty around the three-hour construction and fifteen-minute verification estimates.

Reproducibility and statistical reporting remain incomplete despite the detailed prompts. Exact model snapshots, reasoning settings, and execution budgets are insufficiently specified, while most reasoning-model tasks use one sample and headline comparisons lack uncertainty estimates. Overall, the contribution has clear merit, but unresolved measurement validity prevents a confident acceptance recommendation.

strengths: Significance: Automating the creation of backend specifications, functional tests, and security tests addresses a useful bottleneck in maintaining code-security benchmarks. The 40 new scenarios and evaluation across 14 frameworks provide a substantial practical contribution.

Originality: The combination of specification-grounded refinement and contrastive vulnerable/patched reference solutions is a meaningful systems contribution beyond simply prompting an LLM to generate tests.

Soundness: Evaluation includes comparison against expert-written tests on identical implementations, inspection of all 71 generated security tests for BAXBENCH, alternative reference frameworks, and a disjoint-model construction ablation. Rank correlations of 0.93 for functional correctness and 0.91 for secure correctness support the stability of broad model rankings.

Presentation and reproducibility: The pipeline is clearly organized, with extensive pseudocode, prompts, worked examples, refinement limits, and failure analyses. These details substantially aid understanding and reimplementation.

Limitations and ethics: The paper candidly discusses incomplete coverage, audit limitations, and dual-use implications. Excluding unreliable resource-exhaustion tests from the main evaluation, while reporting their effects separately, is a sensible methodological decision.
weaknesses: Soundness—invalid score-error bound: Appendix A.7 claims that 96.77% exploit soundness implies that correcting false positives could increase sec_pass@1 by at most 3.23%. This does not follow: Table 7 aggregates human judgments about tests, whereas sec_pass@1 aggregates implementations passing all tests. A single flawed test can affect many implementations. The same section incorrectly states that inadequate exploit generalization would underestimate sec_pass@1; missed vulnerabilities instead inflate it. The paper needs implementation-level reassessment of questionable tests to establish score reliability.

Soundness—an illustrated exploit does not establish the claimed end-to-end vulnerability: In Figures 17 and 23–24, SVGBadgeForge returns SVG as text/plain, and the XSS test detects injected markup in that response. The proposed attack assumes a downstream consumer inserts the output into an executable browser context, but that behavior is not specified or exercised. This demonstrates markup injection under an additional threat-model assumption, rather than an end-to-end XSS exploit of the specified backend. The distinction matters for the central claim of sound security measurement.

Validation remains insufficient to resolve these concerns. The systematic audit covers only six newly generated scenarios and six existing scenarios, with three authors and one coworker as raters. Its 124 security judgments are not 124 independently audited exploits. The original 71-test audit uses one author. These provide useful evidence, but neither establishes the impact of residual false positives across the released benchmark; the audit results also combine tests with and without the excluded CWE-400 category.

Methodological attribution: The ablations vary models and reference frameworks but do not isolate the proposed reliability mechanisms. Comparisons against direct generation, execution-only refinement, and refinement without contrastive solutions would establish whether the additional machinery improves soundness or coverage at comparable cost. LLM-generated and LLM-judged contrastive pairs can otherwise share mistaken assumptions.

Several claims exceed the evidence. The disjoint-model experiment supports ranking robustness, not inherently contamination-free evaluation. Endpoint count also provides only partial difficulty control: the strongest model scores 36%, 40%, and 25% on EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD, respectively. The 12-fold human-effort reduction lacks a documented matched timing study establishing the three-hour construction and fifteen-minute verification estimates.

Reproducibility and statistical reporting could be stronger: exact model snapshots, inference budgets, uncertainty across scenario samples, and the cost of discarded generation attempts are insufficiently documented. With only ten scenarios in each outer difficulty split and one completion for reasoning models, uncertainty is especially relevant to comparisons between close scores.
